specPoints.text: understand how genes exist in alternative forms called alleles which give rise to differences in inherited characteristics

primer.text: Genes rarely come in just one flavour. This note unpacks what an allele is, why almost every cell in your body holds two of them for each gene, and how the small DNA differences between versions feed the variation that inheritance acts on. A bitter-tasting chemical called PTC provides a tidy illustration.

lessons.title: Alternative Forms of a Gene
lessons.opening: Every gene can show up in several versions called alleles: their DNA base sequences differ slightly, and because you inherit one chromosome copy from each parent you carry two alleles for nearly every gene, one maternal and one paternal.
keyPoints: A gene is a DNA section that codes for one specific protein.
Alleles are alternative versions of the same gene, differing in base sequence.
Body cells hold two alleles per gene, one inherited from each parent.
Different allele combinations produce variation in inherited characteristics.

low.restatement: You carry two versions of most genes because each parent handed you one chromosome copy.
low.analogy: A gene is a recipe; alleles are the slightly different editions of that same recipe.
low.examPointer: Quote the definition cleanly: alleles are alternative forms of the same gene.

medium.restatement: The two allele copies differ in a few DNA letters, so each can steer the protein slightly differently.
medium.analogy: Two printings of one book with a few typos in different spots: same story, subtly different text.
medium.examPointer: Link alleles to variation explicitly; examiners want the chain from base differences to different characteristics.

check.stem: How many alleles for a typical gene does a human body cell carry?

options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
A single allele would mean only one parental copy, which body cells do not have.
Four copies would double the true chromosome count.
That number counts chromosome pairs, not alleles of one gene.

check.stem: Where do the two alleles of one gene come from?

options.text: One from the mother and one from the father
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Paternal inheritance supplies only one of the two chromosome copies.
Maternal inheritance likewise supplies only one copy.
The copies are inherited, not newly built by the body.

check.stem: What actually differs between two alleles of the same gene?

options.text: The sequence of DNA bases differs slightly between them
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Alleles of one gene sit at the same position on its pair of chromosomes.
Dominance is a separate concept; not every gene's alleles differ in dominance.
Allele versions are near-equals, not double-length copies.

check.stem: Why do alleles matter for inherited characteristics?

options.text: Different base sequences can code for different protein versions, giving different characteristic variants
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: They change the number of chromosomes
options.explanation: Alleles are versions of one gene, not extra chromosomes.

options.text: They decide the sex of offspring
options.explanation: Sex is set by a whole chromosome pair, not by typical gene alleles.

options.text: They store energy for the cell
options.explanation: Energy storage is not a gene's role.

check.stem: What does the single gene behind PTC tasting demonstrate about alleles?

options.text: One gene can exist as two alleles that give different traits
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
The trait follows inherited alleles, not training.
The vegetable merely carries related bitter compounds.

options.text: Every gene has more than two alleles
options.explanation: The example shows a gene with exactly two.

check.stem: State what an allele is in terms of a gene.
check.modelAnswer: An allele is an alternative form, or version, of the same gene, differing slightly in its DNA base sequence.

check.stem: Explain why humans carry two alleles for each gene.
check.modelAnswer: Humans inherit two chromosome copies, one from each parent, so each gene is present as two alleles.

check.stem: Explain how having two alleles per gene contributes to variation within a species.
check.modelAnswer: Because the two alleles can differ in base sequence, they can code for protein variants, so different allele pairings give different characteristics across individuals.

check.stem: A couple are both tasters for PTC. Using the idea of alleles, describe what each parent contributes to their child for this gene.
check.modelAnswer: Each parent contributes one allele of the PTC tasting gene, so the child receives two alleles, one maternal and one paternal.

glossary.definition: A section of a DNA molecule that codes for one specific protein.
An alternative version of a gene, differing slightly in its base sequence.
The order of chemical letters along a strand of DNA.
Differences in inherited characteristics between members of a species.
